Three terminal apps I would not work without: lazygit, yazi and VisiData

A terminal user interface (TUI) sits between a command line and a graphical app: you see the state of things and move with the keyboard. Three of them carry a large part of my daily work.

lazygit: version control at the speed of thought

lazygit shows files, branches, commits and the stash in one screen. Staging single hunks or lines, amending a commit, cherry-picking or resolving a conflict takes a few keys instead of a long command. It also opens inside Neovim through a plugin, so I commit without leaving the editor. One small configuration detail: I point its clipboard commands at tmux, so copying works the same over SSH, which matters when I work on a remote machine.

yazi: a file manager that knows my data

yazi is a fast file manager with previews for almost everything: images, PDFs, archives, tables. It is extensible with small Lua plugins and I added a few for data work:

  • Enter on a .duckdb file opens it in the DuckDB shell, directories and other files behave as usual.
  • Diff the selected file with the hovered one, on one key.
  • A space menu with my custom tools, and quick archive and extract commands.

VisiData: a spreadsheet for the terminal

VisiData opens CSV, Parquet, JSON, SQLite and many other formats as a sheet, and handles millions of rows without complaint. The two keys I use most are Shift-F, which turns a column into a frequency table, and Shift-I, which describes the whole sheet with summary statistics. It is the fastest way I know to answer "what is actually in this file?" before writing any code.

VisiData is written in Python and is easy to extend, so I added some commands of my own for the questions I keep asking:

  • Association heatmaps across all columns: Pearson r for numeric pairs, Cramér's V for categorical ones and the variance explained (η²) for mixed pairs.
  • OLS regression and a decision tree on the current sheet.
  • Deduplication, binning and automatic column typing.
  • Terminal charts drawn with plotext.

What they have in common

All three show the whole picture first and let me act on it with a couple of keys. And because they are terminal apps, they work exactly the same on my laptop and on the computer at home that I reach from my phone, as described in the post about the terminal.
